content.p: The Outlaws Motorcycle Club grew out of the bars and garages of the Chicago area and became one of the best-known motorcycle clubs in the United States. For some, it is a brotherhood built on bikes. For federal prosecutors, in a series of cases stretching from the 1990s to 2018, it was an organization whose leaders planned assaults and killings against rival bikers, chiefly the Hells Angels. Defendants in those cases were tried and convicted individually; prosecutors, not the club's members, supplied most of the descriptions of the club as an enterprise.
This account follows the club from its Illinois beginnings through the trials that shaped its public reputation, and ends with a killing on a UK motorway that showed how far the feud reached.
content.h2: A club with two founding stories
content.p: Sources do not agree on when the Outlaws began. An online timeline says the McCook Outlaws Motorcycle Club formed at Matilda's Bar in McCook, southwest of Chicago, and calls it the oldest outlaw club still operating. A former Chicago chapter president who testified in Florida in 2003 likewise placed the club's origins in the Chicago area in 1935. The Chicago Sun-Times puts the founding in McCook "in the 1930s".

The FBI told a different story in 1995. Agent Robert S. Brown testified in a Tampa courtroom that it was not until 1959 that some Chicago bikers took the skull-and-crossed-pistons patch that Marlon Brando wore in the 1953 film The Wild One and called themselves the Outlaws Motorcycle Club. The two accounts are not necessarily in conflict, since one may describe an earlier local club and the other the group that wore the patch, but the pages do not say so, and the dates are recorded here as the sources gave them.

Brown also testified that the club reached Florida about ten years after the 1959 date, with James "Big Jim" Nolan founding the South Florida chapter in 1967 and then expanding by taking over smaller clubs. He said the Tampa chapter began in 1975, and that the Outlaws then had 31 chapters in 13 states, seven chapters in Canada and others in Australia and France. Defence lawyers objected that Brown's knowledge came from other officers and from former Outlaws seeking leniency, and that he had no training as a historian or sociologist.

The Chicago club was documented from the inside in the 1960s. The photographer Danny Lyon, who had begun studying at the University of Chicago in 1959, followed the Outlaws for four years from 1963 and was a full member in 1965 and 1966, according to the Chicago Reader. His book The Bikeriders, first published in 1968, recorded races, runs, club meetings and even a funeral, and is credited with inspiring Easy Rider. Lyon said Hunter S. Thompson, who had spent a year with the Hells Angels, advised him not to join the Outlaws and to wear a helmet. His reply was that he joined and seldom wore one.

The Reader's account also supplies the origin of the name "one percenter" that the club still claims: a supposed claim by the American Motorcycle Association that 99 percent of its members were law-abiding.

The rivalry with the Hells Angels is the thread running through nearly every case. Accounts of how it began differ. Agent Brown told the Tampa jury that two New York bikers who had left a third club split, one joining the Angels and the other the Outlaws in Chicago, and that when the Outlaws recruit returned to New York in 1973 the Angels beat him. The Guardian wrote in 2008 that the clubs' first clashes came in the 1960s, after three Hells Angels were killed in the United States. The same timeline describes the feud hardening into open war across the US and Canada, with the Outlaws' motto ADIOS standing for "Angels Die In Outlaw States".

Brown testified that many Outlaws wear a patch or tattoo reading AHAMD, which he said means All Hell's Angels Must Die. Another slogan, "Snitches are a dying breed", was recalled in later testimony by a former member, who said such sayings were not jokes but promises.

In 2003 in Florida, Carl "Jay" Warneke testified against James "Frank" Wheeler, described in the Tampa Bay Times as the alleged former national and international head of the Outlaws, who faced racketeering charges. The newspaper's report does not give the outcome. Warneke, who joined in 1988 and rose to president of the Chicago chapter, was himself serving a double life sentence and was hoping his cooperation might shorten it. He called 1994 a "very busy year" of bombings, killings and battles with the Hells Angels and their affiliate, the Hell's Henchmen.

According to Warneke, about 40 Outlaws met 25 Hells Angels at a public race track in Lancaster, New York. He said an Outlaw leader known as Buffalo Wally and the Angels' leader Mike Quale both died in the fighting, which began with fists and then escalated to gunfire and knives. He also said Outlaws later left a car rigged with a large bomb outside the Chicago clubhouse of the Hell's Henchmen and, weeks afterwards, burned what remained of the building. Warneke said he was arrested in 1997, charged with taking part in Quale's death and another killing, and convicted in 2000, after which he began cooperating. This is the testimony of a cooperating witness with an interest in the outcome, and the pages record it as his account.

In 2001 a federal indictment accused six Outlaws from Illinois and Wisconsin of bombings, drugs and murder in the 1990s, among them the deaths of two Hells Angels, the Chicago Sun-Times reported. By 2018, the five co-defendants had been convicted and had served their time. The sixth, Orville "Orvie" Cochran, had vanished as the indictment came in.

The indictment, as summarized by FOX6 Milwaukee, covered a period from January 1988 to at least May 2001 and alleged murder, attempted murder, arson, extortion and drug trafficking across five states: Illinois, Indiana, Minnesota, New York and Wisconsin. It said that until about 1993 the Outlaws controlled the Wisconsin, Illinois and Indiana territory, with the nearest Hells Angels chapter in Minneapolis. In late 1993 or early 1994 the Outlaws' leaders came to believe that the Angels might be gaining a foothold by patching over an affiliate club, and agreed to assault its members.

The indictment described two events. At a June 1994 event at the Illiana Motor Speedway in Schererville, Indiana, Outlaws arrived armed, with two vans carrying weapons, intending, according to the document, to assault rival bikers. No rivals appeared, and a police stop of one van led to the discovery of weapons. In June 1996, Outlaws travelled to a dragway in Morocco, Indiana, with firearms hidden in two surplus police-style vehicles. Rain cancelled the event, and again no rivals came.

Cochran was then the president of the Chicago Southside chapter, which the Sun-Times calls the original and carries "a certain mystique". After the indictment he disappeared. He was arrested in April 2017 in Evergreen Park, Illinois, for shoplifting a back brace from a Meijer store. In the 2018 report the Sun-Times said it was not known where he had been, and that by one account he left with $35,000.

The same report said authorities regarded him as a prime suspect in the 1999 killing of fellow Outlaw Thomas "West Side Tommy" Stimac, who was found shot to death at his home in Lemont Township. The paper's sources said Stimac had been dating Cochran's former girlfriend. Cochran has not been reported charged with that killing in the pages consulted. A year after Stimac's death, Cochran himself was shot at outside the South Side clubhouse at 25th and Rockwell, in what police believed was retaliation, and he survived.

In October 2018 Cochran pleaded guilty to one count of the four-count indictment, racketeering conspiracy, facing up to 20 years. In a 2021 prosecution filing quoted by the Sun-Times, he admitted conspiring to assault and murder rival bikers at the Schererville and Morocco events. He was sentenced to five years. After catching COVID-19 in prison, he won a judge's order for early release in 2021, six months before his scheduled August date, over prosecutors' objections that his sentence was already light.

A second major case reached the top of the organization. A June 2010 indictment charged leaders and members of the Outlaws in Wisconsin, Maine, Montana, North Carolina, Tennessee, South Carolina and Virginia. The Justice Department said that Jack Rosga, known as "Milwaukee Jack", the club's national president, was found guilty on 21 December 2010 of conspiring to engage in racketeering and conspiring to commit violence in aid of racketeering. In April 2011 Judge Henry E. Hudson sentenced him to 20 years. By then 27 people had been charged and 20 had pleaded guilty or been convicted.

The release said court records showed planned shows of force against rival clubs at events from 2006 to 2010, including in Virginia, Florida and North Carolina. It said the Outlaws opened a clubhouse in Rock Hill, South Carolina, in 2008, in territory long held by the Hells Angels. It also said two Outlaws were assaulted in Connecticut by Hells Angels in September 2009 and that, in October 2009, a Hells Angels member was shot outside his clubhouse in Canaan, Maine, in what the release called an alleged attempted murder. In April 2010, it said, Outlaws from Wisconsin crossed into Minnesota during a charity ride, beat Hells Angels members and took their patches. Witnesses at trial testified that the club regularly used and distributed drugs.

The feud also reached the UK. In August of the year before the verdicts, on the road home from the Bulldog Bash festival in Warwickshire, the Hells Angel Gerry Tobin was shot dead on the M40 as a car pulled alongside his motorcycle, according to the Guardian. In November 2008 seven members of the south Warwickshire chapter of the Outlaws were convicted of murder or had pleaded guilty. Sean Creighton, identified by the Guardian as holding one of the two guns used, pleaded guilty; the Guardian named the others convicted as Simon Turner, Dane Garside, Dean Taylor, Malcolm Bull, Karl Garside and Ian Cameron.

Prosecutor Timothy Raggatt told the jury Tobin was targeted "not because of who he was, but because of what he was". Police believed the attack was probably sanctioned at a high level in the club, though that was an officer's belief and not a finding. A separate Outlaw, David Melles, was jailed for twelve years for keeping an armoury of weapons.

The court findings reviewed here rest on convictions and guilty pleas of individuals. The Justice Department's own phrase, "a highly organized criminal enterprise", comes from a press release about the Rosga case. A 2012 sweep in Illinois, Indiana and Ohio led to the arrest of 42 members, for alleged money laundering, extortion, drug offences, witness tampering and illegal gambling, the Reader reported, without giving the outcome.
